title: 1 Timothy 6:1–2
context: Paul addresses believers already living under a first-century yoke: honor masters so that God’s name and the teaching are not blasphemed. Those with believing masters must not despise them as mere equals; they should serve all the better, because those who benefit are believing and beloved. Teach and exhort these things.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on honor under a yoke, the Name that must not be reviled, and believing masters who are brothers, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Let servants under the yoke - Of heathen masters. Account them worthy of all honour - All the honour due from a servant to a master. Lest the name of God and his doctrine be blasphemed - As it surely will, if they do otherwise. Let them not despise them - Pay them the less honour or obedience. Because they are brethren - And in that respect on a level with them. But rather do them service - Serve them so much the more diligently. Because they are joint partakers of the great benefit - Salvation.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on 1 Tim 6:1–2)

reformed.quote: They ought to obey unbelieving masters, in order that the name of God and the gospel may not be evil spoken of; as if God, whom we worship, incited us to rebellion, and as if the gospel rendered obstinate those who ought to be subject to others. The name of brother may be thought to constitute equality. Paul argues, on the contrary, that they ought the more willingly to subject themselves to believing masters, because they acknowledge them to be children of God, and are bound to them by brotherly love, and are partakers of the same grace.

verses.text: Let as many as are bondservants under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honor, that the name of God and the doctrine not be blasphemed.
verses.arminianNotes:
Paul speaks pastorally to Christians already under a first-century yoke. Honor is aimed at protecting the Name and the teaching from mockery, not at baptizing the institution. The gospel's public reputation is at stake in how believers inhabit a hard setting.

Arminian interpreters hear a call the Spirit enables: costly respect so that Christ is not blamed. Grace that saves also trains a holy witness. It is counsel about the Name among watching neighbors.
verses.reformedNotes:
The aim is explicit: that God's name and the doctrine not be blasphemed. Paul does not pause to theorize the social order; he shepherds people already in it toward honor that adorns the gospel.

God cares how His Word looks in a household. Obedience here is witness under providence, not a brief for the yoke itself. The church's first loyalty is the Name; contempt that makes the gospel look rebellious would slander the very Lord who bought them.

verses.text: Those who have believing masters, let them not despise them because they are brothers, but rather let them serve them, because those who partake of the benefit are believing and beloved. Teach and exhort these things.
verses.arminianNotes:
Brotherhood in Christ is no illusion: believing masters are brothers, believers, and beloved. That new family must not be twisted into contempt. Serve all the better, Paul says, because the ones who benefit belong to the same Savior. Teach and exhort these things: practical holiness is not a footnote to faith.

The gospel sincerely creates one household of faith without erasing the setting they inhabit. Greater grace is needed, as Wesley noted, to honor a brother than a stranger. Love for the beloved, not a defense of rank, is the motive.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the name brother might seem to cancel dominion; Paul argues the opposite from shared grace. They are children of God together, bound by brotherly love, partakers of the same adoption. Service should be better, not worse, when the beneficiary is beloved in the faith.

The new family in Christ is the deeper fact. God joins people across stations in one salvation; that bond is reason for faithful work and for refusing disdain. Timothy must teach and urge this, because the church's common life is a gospel argument.
